stories.title: Andhra landfall or Tamil Nadu strike? Conflicting forecasts cloud Cyclone Akvan's path
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: IMD expects Cyclone Akvan to make landfall along the Andhra Pradesh coast, while private weather forecasters point to a possible Tamil Nadu strike between Chennai and Cuddalore.
Will Cyclone Akvan strike Tamil Nadu or move towards Andhra Pradesh?
With the storm's projected trajectory subject to conflicting forecasts, residents along the eastern coast are grappling with uncertainty about where it could eventually make landfall.

While the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has maintained that the system is likely to cross the Andhra Pradesh coast, private weather forecasters suggest the cyclone could instead make landfall somewhere between Chennai and Cuddalore.

The conflicting assessments have triggered confusion, particularly among residents in coastal Tamil Nadu, who are trying to understand the potential threat and whether they need to prepare for the cyclone's impact.
According to the IMD's assessment on Sunday, a depression over the southeast and adjoining southwest Bay of Bengal is likely to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm by Tuesday.
The system is expected to move towards the Andhra Pradesh coast around Thursday.
The weather department also released a projected trajectory indicating that the cyclone would travel along the Tamil Nadu coast before making landfall in Andhra Pradesh.
However, private weather enthusiasts have offered a different assessment, suggesting a possible southward shift in the system's path that could bring it towards the Tamil Nadu coastline.
Dr VR Durai of the Regional Meteorological Centre (RMC), Chennai, told DT Next that IMD scientists rely on multiple weather prediction models to assess a cyclone's movement and projected trajectory.
These include the Multi Model Ensemble (MME) model and several global weather forecasting models.
Durai said that both RMC and IMD scientists had forecast an Andhra Pradesh landfall for Cyclone Akvan.

stories.headline: Four nations urge Israel to allow Gaza aid amid flood crisis
stories.title: Four nations urge Israel to allow Gaza aid amid flood crisis
stories.summary: Four nations urge Israel to allow Gaza aid amid flood crisis
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: With heavy rains and flooding adding to the suffering of displaced Palestinians, Australia, Canada, Italy and the United Kingdom have urged Israel to immediately lift restrictions on humanitarian aid and allow essential supplies to enter Gaza without delay.

In a joint statement issued on Sunday, the foreign ministers of the four countries warned that thousands of families were facing increasingly desperate conditions as winter approaches, with many left without adequate shelter after recent floods destroyed or swept away makeshift tents.
The ministers said around 150,000 tents and other essential relief supplies were being held at the border, preventing them from reaching people in need.

“People in Gaza desperately need shelter and humanitarian assistance,” the statement said, calling on the Israeli government to ensure immediate, rapid and unimpeded humanitarian access throughout the territory.
The appeal comes amid a deepening humanitarian crisis, with heavy rainfall worsening living conditions for millions of displaced Palestinians.
According to the United Nations, more than 1.9 million people have been displaced in Gaza, many of them forced to flee their homes multiple times.
The Global Shelter Cluster, a humanitarian coordination body, estimated that Gaza needs at least 1.7 million mattresses and 121,000 tents to help residents withstand the cold and rainy winter season.
The four nations stressed that the situation could still be addressed if humanitarian supplies were allowed to enter without further delays.
Beyond the shortage of shelter, the prolonged conflict and restrictions on essential goods have pushed hundreds of thousands of Palestinians into poverty.
Rising prices, shrinking incomes and widespread destruction have further undermined access to basic necessities.

The joint statement followed a similar warning from the UN Humanitarian Country Team for the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which said recent storms had flooded, damaged or destroyed thousands of family shelters and disrupted critical services.
The European Union also voiced grave concern over the humanitarian situation on Saturday, urging Israel to allow immediate aid deliveries and reopen all border crossings into Gaza.

stories.headline: Trump's tariffs cast shadow over APEC talks
stories.title: Trump's tariffs cast shadow over APEC talks
stories.summary: Shenzhen: APEC nations account for just over half of global commerce, but geopolitical rivalries and US President Donald Trump's trade war -- even after a midterm drubbing -- mean an agenda of limited ambition at this week's summit.All located around the Pacific Rim, the organisation's 21 members gathering in Shenzhen include the United States and China as well as Japan, Russia, Canada, Mexico, Australia and Indonesia.But "having China serve as host in an institution that includes the United States and Russia has not been a recipe for success," said Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation in Singapore."All three are at odds with one another and geopolitical rivalries that cross many members have made cooperation on even relatively benign topics harder than ever," Elms wrote in a research note.Important figures including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent skipped an APEC finance ministers' meeting in Hong Kong in October, depriving other members of "the opportunity to connect to a key official from the United States", Elms said.China has also been making "unhelpful changes" to APEC processes, like moving some meetings online and not confirming until very late in the process to timings of some key events, she added.Trump 'unleashed' At the same time there is no sign of a reversal in Trump's tariff blitz even after the Democrats won control of both houses of Congress in midterm elections on November 3.The US Supreme Court struck down a host of Trump's customs duties in February.But Washington has since cited inadequate efforts to combat forced labour as grounds for imposing new tariffs -- as high as 12.5 percent -- on 60 economies, including APEC members in Asia and Latin America.Meanwhile, sector-specific tariffs on steel, automobiles, and timber remain in effect.Trump is "doubling down," said Joshua Kurlantzick, senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), and Congress "can't do much about Trump's trade and tariffs, and I don't think Trump is going to change.""He doesn't care also about whether his policies impact GOP favourability, so that kind of makes him unleashed to do whatever he wants in a way," Kurlantzick told AFP, referring to the Republicans.Reducing dependance This has added to the impetus for other countries to deepen trade relations without the world's biggest economy.Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Saturday that Ottawa had concluded negotiations for a free-trade pact with the Philippines.He added that a broader agreement was also in the works with the entirety of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).The pacts were "part of a strategy of developing a dense web of reliable partners to create more opportunities... and reducing our relative reliance on the United States," Carney said.Brazil's newly re-elected President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, while not an APEC member, sounded a similar note at the ASEAN gathering in Manila on Sunday."Brazil has learned an extraordinary lesson after the US decided to impose tariffs (on other countries)," Lula told reporters."Instead of weeping or begging the US government... to have pity on us, we decided to look for other partners for us to sell and for us to buy from," he said, noting that trade with Indonesia and Vietnam had jumped 15 and 13 percent, respectively.The Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) -- a free-trade agreement encompassing China, Southeast Asian nations, and other regional partners such as Japan, Australia, and South Korea -- has meanwhile set long-term targets for tariff reductions.However, the agreement's provisions "suffer from weaker enforcement and dispute settlement mechanisms," said Nick Marro, principal Asia economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit."While the drive to expand and deepen RCEP will stay, the pact will offer middle powers relatively limited shelter in an increasingly fractious geopolitical landscape-especially amid rising US protectionism and the continued global spillover of China's economic imbalances," he told AFP.

stories.headline: Clarion call for environmental protection
stories.title: Clarion call for environmental protection
stories.summary: Jammu and Kashmir is facing serious environmental issues and there is urgency to come up with solutions to arrest further deterioration of our fragile ecosystem. It was heartening when people from different walks of life during two special dialogues organised by Nigeen Lake Conservation Organisation (NLCO) stressed on sustainable tourism and environmental conservation in Kashmir. The dialogues—Rethinking Kashmir’s Tourism Model: A Vision for Eco-Friendly Tourism by 2030 and Environment and the Way Forward brought senior government officials, tourism professionals, academicians, environmentalists, civil society representatives and other stakeholders under one roof and brainstorm on sustainable tourism and protection of Kashmir’s natural heritage. Concerns were expressed on deterioration of J&K’s natural resources due to ill-planning and vandalisation of lakes, wetlands, forests and mountains in absence of regulation. Participants minced no words to express their resentment to excessive concretisation of Kashmir’s popular tourist resorts. A senior government official pointed out that a union minister was shocked to see “concrete monsters” on both sides on the way from Narbal to famous ski-resort Gulmarg and expressed disappointment over disappearance of a popular tree line and vast stretches of agricultural fields. Tourists visit Kashmir to spend time away from the hustle and bustle of their native places. The concern shown by our think tanks is right. Do tourists visit to see our polluted water bodies, diminishing forests and concrete structures? No. They just want to see and feel our pristine nature and breathe a fresh whiff of air! Other stakeholders lamented over gradual loss of Kashmir’s hydrological system due to illegal mining and rising pollution levels. While an environmental expert highlighted serious threats to our glaciers due to pollution and rising temperature and glacial lakes which are like “ticking time bombs.” And there was a clarion call for practical efforts to ensure environmental protection. Speakers stressed that environmental protection must remain central to J&K’s development planning. They called for practical interventions, institutional coordination, community participation and sustained collective action to address the region’s ecological challenges. Suggesting NLCO’s initiatives in Nigeen, Gilsar and Khushalsar lakes as a model of peoples’ participation, speakers called for restoration of water bodies, revival of traditional springs, and scientific waste management. A resolution was passed for conservation of Anchar lake in Srinagar which is facing threat of extinction due to unabated encroachments, pollution and siltation. Anchar lake receives major lease of its waters from Dal lake through Nallah Amir Khan via Gilsar and Khushalsar lakes. A network of channels from the cold water nallah Sindh enters the lake on its western shore forming a delta. The lake is also fed by springs within the basin and along the periphery. It finally merges with Jhelum at Sangam. However, unabated pollution, siltation coupled with extensive encroachments, has severely affected its flora and fauna. From 19.54 sq.km a century ago, the lake has been reduced to 6 sq.km, out of which 3.6 sq.km is marsh. The resolution moved by NLCO chairman Manzoor Ahmad Wangnoo calls for creation of Anchar Development Authority — a dedicated, empowered body to own the lake’s restoration. Most of the speakers stressed home composting of wet waste to reduce the burden of municipal solid waste treatment facilities. Suggestions were dished out on use of solar energy and eco-friendly measures to reduce carbon footprints. It was good to hear speakers, mostly tourism stakeholders, call for sustainable tourism. They stressed that Kashmir’s tourism future lies not in volume, but in value and stressed on respecting the carrying capacity of tourist resorts and protection of natural resources. Rising above economic considerations, they visualised a thriving, eco-conscious tourism economy that leaves the landscape better than it found it! Former Tourism Minister Tasduq Mufti in his special address stated that the event had provided an opportunity to understand environmental issues confronting J&K. He rightly said that it is high time to find solutions to environmental problems. “We have taken it upon ourselves to make it waste-free, to make it a place where children and old people can come and walk and see this Valley as beautiful as it can be. The possibilities are endless. We just need to imagine.” We must note that J&K ranks third among the Himalayan areas which are vulnerable to climate change and fall in the highest seismic zones. The region is a multi-hazard prone Himalayan region which is vulnerable to natural disasters especially earthquake, floods, landslides, windstorms and soil erosion besides there is looming threat of Glacial Lake Flood Outbursts. J&K has been facing serious effects of climate change. From the last several years there has been less snowfall in peak winter period coupled with rain deficit in rains in summer. In between there are incessant rains triggered by cloudbursts. This has severely affected irrigated agriculture, horticultural productivity, and hydropower generation, thereby posing serious challenges to the region’s water security and climate resilience. Our glaciers too are retreating fast due to rising temperature and pollution. Even traces of Black Carbon have been detected on many of our glaciers. Our natural resources are under stress due to rapid urbanisation. In this scenario, more such programs must be organised where officers and stakeholders sit together to come up with solutions to our environmental problems. Much has changed in Kashmir in the last three decades. The pristine Kashmir that was especially in the 1980s is totally missing. It’s really a Paradise Lost. We have not spared even Kashmir’s skyline and blocked view of mountains by skyscrapers. We need to wake up before it’s too late and save our environment from further deterioration. Author is Executive Editor, Greater Kashmir

stories.headline: 84% of Amarnath route slopes landslide-prone
stories.title: 84% of Amarnath route slopes landslide-prone
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 15: More than 84 percent of mapped slope facets along the Amarnath Yatra corridor fall in moderate-to-high landslide susceptibility zones, with 16.2 percent classified as highly susceptible, according to a study published in the international journal Scientific Reports on November 10. The study, 'Geological and Climatic controls on Landslide Susceptibility and Hazard Along the Amarnath pilgrimage corridor, Kashmir Himalaya,' found that 68.1 percent of the mapped slope facets fall in the moderate-susceptibility category, while 15.7 percent have low susceptibility. Researchers mapped 1469 slope facets across the study area. Together, moderate and high-susceptibility zones accounted for 84.3 percent of the mapped facets. The figures represent the distribution of slope facets and not the share of the corridor's total geographical area. The findings assume significance amid rising yatri numbers in recent years and concerns over the safety of the annual yatra to the high-altitude cave shrine. According to government data, the physical yatra was cancelled in 2021 due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Around 3.60 lakh yatris visited the shrine in 2022, rising to approximately 4.45 lakh in 2023 and more than 5.12 lakh in 2024. More than 4.14 lakh devotees undertook the yatra in 2025, while over 4.5 lakh visited the shrine in 2026. The study covers the Baltal-Amarnath Cave-Panjtarni-Poshpathri corridor in the upper Sind catchment of the Himalaya. The terrain ranges from about 6500 feet to 14,300 feet above sea level and comprises steep slopes, fragile geological formations, mountain streams, roads, and seasonal settlements. Researchers documented 49 landslide occurrences along the corridor, including 28 debris flows, 15 rockfalls, two debris slides, two rockslides, one creep zone, and one rock topple. An overlay of the landslide inventory on the susceptibility map showed that 35 of the 49 occurrences, or 71.4 percent, were recorded in areas classified as highly susceptible. Another 10 occurred in moderately susceptible areas and four in low-susceptibility zones. The assessment used 18 conditioning factors, including slope gradient, elevation, geological formations, drainage conditions, land cover, soil characteristics, and proximity to roads. Researchers prepared detailed geological maps at a scale of 1:10,000, combining high-resolution satellite imagery, field investigations, geotechnical testing, and climate records. They also examined 27 sites using Rock Mass Rating and Slope Mass Rating systems, along with kinematic analysis. The model recorded area-under-the-curve values of 0.80 for the success-rate curve and 0.86 for the prediction-rate curve, indicating good model fit and predictive capability. Steep slopes, elevation, proximity to drainage channels, geological formations and structural weaknesses emerged as major controls on landslide susceptibility. Road construction and slope modification were also found to aggravate instability. The corridor has a complex geological setting, comprising phyllite, schist, quartzite, limestone, slate and shale, besides deposits of alluvium, colluvium, moraine and scree. Several formations are intensely folded, faulted, jointed, and deformed. Structural weaknesses associated with the Main Central Thrust and adjoining shear zones further weaken rock masses. Joints, faults and fractures can act as failure surfaces, particularly when combined with steep slopes, thick debris cover, and water saturation. The study found that around 60-70 percent of landslides occurred within 50 metres of roads or other disturbed areas, pointing to the risks associated with construction and human intervention in the fragile mountain terrain. "Extensive slope cutting, blasting, and excavation disturb the natural stress equilibrium of already fragile and highly fractured Himalayan rocks," the researchers state. Such activities can reduce slope support, promote tension cracks and increase surface runoff and water infiltration, raising the likelihood of slope failures. Extreme rainfall a major trigger during Yatra season The study identifies rainfall as a major trigger of landslides during the July-August pilgrimage season, when snow cover across the study area is minimal. Satellite data showed that snow cover falls to around 6 percent in July and about 0.4% in August. With limited direct contribution from snowmelt to slope moisture and streamflow during these months, intense monsoon rainfall becomes a major factor contributing to slope instability. Heavy rainfall can rapidly penetrate loose debris, weathered rocks and already saturated slopes, increasing pore-water pressure and weakening slope stability. This can trigger debris flows, rockfalls and other failures. An analysis of rainfall records from 1994 to 2024 identified 54 extreme rainfall events exceeding 45 millimetres in a single day in the Baltal Valley. Fifteen of these occurred during the monsoon season. The researchers said intense monsoon precipitation poses a greater threat of flash floods, debris flows and landslides. Heavy winter precipitation, which largely falls as snow at higher elevations, can contribute to avalanche-related sediment mobilisation. Rain-on-snow events during spring and early summer can also generate rapid runoff and contribute to slope instability. The study refers to several cloudburst events along the Sonamarg-Baltal-Amarnath-Poshpathri corridor, including incidents in 2015 and 2021 and two events in 2022. The July 8, 2022, cloudburst at Baltal triggered debris-laden floods, reactivated existing landslide scars and caused fresh slope failures. The disaster left 16 people dead and 55 injured. The researchers said rugged topography, fragile geology, steep slopes, narrow valleys and high-intensity rainfall make the Baltal-Amarnath sector particularly vulnerable to flash floods and cascading landslides. The concentration of pilgrims and temporary infrastructure during the yatra further increases exposure to these hazards. Pahalgam records significant warming trend The study also examined long-term climate records from the India Meteorological Department's Pahalgam station for 1980-2024 and found a statistically significant rise in annual mean temperature at a rate of 0.0512 degrees Celsius per year. Annual maximum temperature increased by 0.0556 degrees Celsius per year, while minimum temperature rose by 0.0524 degrees Celsius per year. Annual precipitation showed a declining tendency of 5.15 mm per year, although the trend was not statistically significant. The researchers said the warming trend could affect snow and glacier dynamics, soil-moisture conditions, water availability and meltwater generation in the region. stories.headline: Iran warns of widening conflict, accuses regional states of aiding US strikes
stories.title: Iran warns of widening conflict, accuses regional states of aiding US strikes
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 15: Iran has warned that the geographical scope of the ongoing conflict could expand if the United States makes what it called a mistake, while accusing regional countries of facilitating American military strikes against Tehran. According to Al Jazeera, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said Tehran had documented evidence of regional countries assisting US attacks on Iran and had raised the matter through diplomatic channels. "All the cases that indicate the role of the countries of the region in helping the US to attack Iran have been documented," Baghaei said, adding that Tehran would pursue the matter seriously, reports Al Jazeera. He alleged that missiles, drones and aircraft launched from military bases in these countries, along with logistical support provided to US forces, demonstrated their involvement. Baghaei also defended Iran's attacks on neighbouring countries, invoking Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises the right to self-defence. "No action has been taken by Iran against the sovereignty of these countries," he claimed, insisting that Iranian strikes were "purely defensive in nature" and targeted only US military bases and assets used to attack Iran. Bahrain's military, meanwhile, said its air defence systems had thwarted what it described as "treacherous" Iranian attacks and condemned Tehran's "systematic aggression" against the Gulf kingdom. Al Jazeera reported that this was the second time in three days that Iran had launched drones at US military assets in Bahrain, indicating a possible change in Tehran's response to American military operations in the region. On the nuclear issue, Baghaei strongly criticised the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), describing it as "one-sided and biased" after the UN nuclear watchdog again urged Iran to restore access for international inspectors to its nuclear facilities. According to Al Jazeera, Baghaei accused the agency of deliberately leaking information from its reports to Western media and yielding to pressure from Washington. He warned that such political approaches would weaken the agency's professional standing and undermine its credibility. The IAEA, in a report circulated on Friday, called on Tehran to restore access for its inspectors, saying it was essential to monitor Iran's nuclear programme. Iran has permitted only limited inspections since the US and Israel attacked its nuclear facilities in June 2025. Asked whether Tehran would consider a temporary suspension of uranium enrichment or a reduction in enrichment levels as part of a possible agreement with Washington, Baghaei said no such discussions were currently taking place. "No, we are not at that stage at all now," he said, adding that there had been no discussions on the details of the nuclear issue during the current period. Baghaei also accused Washington of lacking seriousness in pursuing peace negotiations, saying the main issue was not whether talks were direct or indirect but whether the US was genuinely willing to advance diplomacy. Referring to the earlier agreement reached between the two sides in June, he said the US had signed the agreement at the highest level, but it had not lasted even two weeks. He was apparently referring to the Islamabad memorandum of understanding, which subsequently collapsed. "The main issue is the seriousness and will to advance diplomacy in its conventional sense," Baghaei said. He added that diplomacy required recognising the rights and interests of the other side rather than seeking unilateral concessions. Meanwhile, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf warned that Tehran would not accept a prolonged situation of "neither war nor peace". He also threatened to expand the geographical scope of the conflict if Washington made what he described as a mistake, Al Jazeera reported.

stories.headline: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
stories.title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
stories.summary: Phnom Penh, Nov 16: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with US President Donald Trump fail to preserve an integrated North American auto industry. Carney's comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where Chinese auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs. “We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions.” Carney said Saturday in Manila, Philippines, that any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry. He said Monday that negotiations with the United States remain his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in the US negotiations, Carney replied: “It's not leverage. But action, reaction.” “If they're not fully utilised in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said of Canada's auto workers and manufacturing assets. “Canada is going to move forward either way.” The Detroit Three — Ford, General Motors and Stellantis — operate factories across Canada, the United States and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the United States from Canada. Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would require proper labour standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles. “It's not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.” Under the January agreement, Canada reduced its 100 per cent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1 per cent, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola. Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada's auto industry and create jobs. The deal drew criticism from Ontario Premier Doug Ford, whose province is the centre of Canada's auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the US market. Trump's tariffs have disrupted Canada's auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant. Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior US officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

stories.title: Statehood restoration, constitutional, democratic rights serve foundation for rebuilding trust: MP Chowdhary Mohammad Ramzan
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 15: The Jammu & Kashmir National Conference Additional General Secretary and MP Choudry Mohammad Ramzan said New Delhi will sooner or later have to reconsider the unconstitutional and undemocratic decisions of August 5, 2019, and restore Jammu and Kashmir’s special constitutional status. He said this while addressing an important party meeting held at the party headquarters, Nawa-e-Subh Complex. The meeting, as per a party statement, was attended by Provincial President Advocate Showkat Ahmad Mir, spokesperson Imran Nabi Dar, Provincial Secretary Syed Tawqeer Ahmad, Provincial President of the Women’s Wing Engineer Sabiya Qadri, Minority Cell Convener Jagdish Singh Azad, Provincial Youth President Mushtaq Mir and other party office-bearers. Chowdhary Mohammad Ramzan said that the unilateral abrogation of J&K’s special constitutional status on August 5, 2019, not only amounted to an injustice against the people of this historic region but also dealt a severe blow to the country’s federal democratic system and constitutional values. He said that Articles 370 and 35A were not merely constitutional provisions but also safeguards for the identity, distinct character, land rights, employment opportunities and constitutional rights of the people of Jammu and Kashmir. He stated that the history of the National Conference is marked by sacrifices and a sustained struggle for protecting the identity, autonomy and special constitutional status of Jammu and Kashmir. "From the leadership of Sher-e-Kashmir Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah to the present day, the party has consistently made sacrifices to safeguard the constitutional rights, dignity and political identity of the people. Despite political challenges, difficult circumstances and adverse conditions, the National Conference has never compromised on its principled position and will not do so in the future either," he added. He further said that the National Conference had raised its voice against the decisions of August 5, 2019, at every democratic, political, constitutional and legal forum. From Parliament to the Supreme Court, the party has continued its struggle for the restoration of the rights of the people of Jammu and Kashmir. He emphasised that the restoration of Articles 370 and 35A remains a fundamental part of the party’s political commitment and struggle. This struggle, he said, is not driven by any political interest or desire for power, but by the need to protect the constitutional rights, collective identity and future of generations to come.

body: The meeting, as per a party statement, was attended by Provincial President Advocate Showkat Ahmad Mir, spokesperson Imran Nabi Dar, Provincial Secretary Syed Tawqeer Ahmad, Provincial President of the Women’s Wing Engineer Sabiya Qadri, Minority Cell Convener Jagdish Singh Azad, Provincial Youth President Mushtaq Mir and other party office-bearers.

Chowdhary Mohammad Ramzan said that the unilateral abrogation of J&K’s special constitutional status on August 5, 2019, not only amounted to an injustice against the people of this historic region but also dealt a severe blow to the country’s federal democratic system and constitutional values.

He said that Articles 370 and 35A were not merely constitutional provisions but also safeguards for the identity, distinct character, land rights, employment opportunities and constitutional rights of the people of Jammu and Kashmir.
He stated that the history of the National Conference is marked by sacrifices and a sustained struggle for protecting the identity, autonomy and special constitutional status of Jammu and Kashmir.

"From the leadership of Sher-e-Kashmir Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah to the present day, the party has consistently made sacrifices to safeguard the constitutional rights, dignity and political identity of the people.

Despite political challenges, difficult circumstances and adverse conditions, the National Conference has never compromised on its principled position and will not do so in the future either," he added.
He further said that the National Conference had raised its voice against the decisions of August 5, 2019, at every democratic, political, constitutional and legal forum.
From Parliament to the Supreme Court, the party has continued its struggle for the restoration of the rights of the people of Jammu and Kashmir.
He emphasised that the restoration of Articles 370 and 35A remains a fundamental part of the party’s political commitment and struggle.
This struggle, he said, is not driven by any political interest or desire for power, but by the need to protect the constitutional rights, collective identity and future of generations to come.

stories.headline: A chainsaw is not a traffic plan
stories.title: A chainsaw is not a traffic plan
stories.summary: In the quiet town of Ganderbal, along the bustling Duderhama Hospital Road, four majestic Chinar trees stand as silent witnesses to a familiar, tragic debate. As traffic bottlenecks grow more frustrating on this vital stretch, a chorus of voices has emerged with a deceptively simple solution: cut down the trees to widen the road. To the commuters stuck in gridlock, the logic appears straightforward. More asphalt equals more space, and more space equals faster movement. Yet, if we pause to examine urban planning history, environmental science, and the sheer reality of human behavior, it becomes clear that axing these four heritage trees is not progress. It is a short-sighted surrender to poor planning — an environmental crime disguised as urban development. I respect opinions, but let’s be honest — why should nature always suffer for our failures? Let us be brutally honest about why these four trees are being targeted. A Chinar cannot hire a lawyer, stage a dharna, or vote in the next election. Over the past two decades, Kashmir has developed a coward’s habit of sacrificing its ecology whenever planning fails — first slicing through Himalayan forests for highways, then burying fertile apple orchards under concrete colonies, and now raising the axe against our heritage Chinars. If widening roads by removing obstacles is truly the answer, why not demolish the illegal shop extensions and boundary walls choking Duderhama Road? Not a single owner would allow it. Otherwise, let’s widen every street and lane in Ganderbal — let’s see how many of you will agree to demolish your own shops and houses for it. Not one. We target trees because they are a soft target. We demand sacrifice only from nature because nature cannot say no. In Kashmir, we have made it a habit — sometimes forests, sometimes apple orchards, now Chinars. Cutting Chinars for road widening is not development; it is environmental destruction. Science has already proved this is not a permanent solution. This is called ‘Induced Demand’, where wider roads only invite more traffic in 3-4 years. This is not activist rhetoric; this is settled transport economics. Research published in journals like the American Economic Review, and studies by transport institutes in the US and India has shown the same principle: when you widen a road, traffic eases for six to twelve months. That very ease encourages more people to buy and use private cars. A ten percent increase in road capacity leads to almost a ten percent increase in vehicle use. Within three to four years, you are back to the same jam, only with more cars and no trees. So ask yourself — if we cut these four Chinars on Duderhama Hospital Road tomorrow and gain six feet, what happens by 2029? More cars will fill that six feet. The bottleneck will return. But those four Chinars, which have taken over a hundred years to build that canopy, will be gone forever. You can lay asphalt in three months. You cannot grow a two-hundred-year-old Chinar in three lifetimes. If we really want a permanent solution, the focus should not be on cutting trees, but on fixing our own greed and indiscipline. Anyone who travels daily from Beehama Chowk to Duderhama Chowk knows that the real cause of the jam is not these four Chinars. The trees stand on the extreme edge, well beyond the carriageway. The real culprit is the complete failure of the Ganderbal district administration and traffic management. Ganderbal is not short of roads; it is short of management. On paper, we already have the full bypass network. There is a road coming from the SP Office which directly joins New Hospital Road, there is a Link Road towards Check, and there is the main Check-Fatehpora Road which goes directly to the DC Office, Safapora-Manasbal and Dab Road via the Nallah Sindh bridge. On the ground, the administration has done nothing to use it. No diversion plan, no signboards, no one-way system, no policing to divert light vehicles through the SP Office Road or the Check Link Road. Instead, every vehicle from Kangan, Beehama and the SP Office is pushed into the same narrow funnel at Duderhama Chowk and then the blame is put on four silent Chinars. What makes this even more absurd is that the most permanent bypass is already lying unused — the existing but neglected Power Canal Road. It starts near Beehama Chowk, runs along the power canal bund, and directly connects to Check-Fatehpora near the Fire Service Station, bypassing Duderhama Chowk and New Hospital Road completely. If restored, more than fifty percent of the pressure on Duderhama Chowk would vanish overnight. This is not a new highway needing hundreds of crores. This is restoration of an existing canal bund allowed to decay. It is cheaper, faster, enduring, and it saves heritage. Power Canal Road restoration is the only permanent solution. Why is it ignored? Because restoring a road requires real work and political will, while cutting a Chinar requires only a chainsaw and an excuse. Let us be clear — there is a bus service in Ganderbal, and there is parking space inside the District Hospital premises. The truth is people do not want to use them. People park on the road even when parking is available inside; because they do not want to walk ten steps. People avoid the bus even when it is available because everyone now wants to come in his own private car, even for a two-kilometre distance. This is not a lack of facility; this is greed, laziness, and a status race. A family of four now owns five cars not out of need, but for show. We have converted a public road into private parking and then we blame the Chinar for blocking the road. The trees stand silently on the side; the cars stand arrogantly in the middle of the road. How is the tree the culprit? Stop exploiting the silence of nature to hide the failures of human planning. Axing heritage trees to fix traffic is not a solution — it is an environmental crime disguised as progress. And here is the irony we ignore — this is a hospital road. A road leading to the District Hospital should be a healing corridor — green, shaded, calm, with lower dust and lower temperature. A single mature Chinar significantly lowers ambient temperature, sequesters a significant amount of carbon dioxide each year, and provides shade for attendants who wait for hours outside. Cutting them to help patients reach faster while making the hospital’s surroundings hotter and dustier is illogical. There is also the myth of “compensatory plantation” — the comforting lie that cutting down a 150-year-old tree is acceptable if we plant ten saplings somewhere else. In ecology, a sapling is not a replacement for an old-growth tree. A newly planted Chinar takes at least thirty to forty years just to establish a meaningful canopy, and over a century to develop the deep root architecture, micro-habitat crevices, and carbon-storage capacity of the trees standing on Duderhama Road. During the critical decades of climate warming that Kashmir is currently experiencing — marked by hotter summers, erratic snowfall, and vanishing glaciers — trading four functioning adult trees for ten fragile saplings is like burning down a library and promising to plant trees to make paper later. A Chinar is protected under the J&K Preservation of Specified Trees Act. You can plant saplings anywhere, but you cannot recreate heritage. The four Chinars on Duderhama Road represent a choice between two visions of Kashmir. One vision views the Valley merely as a transit corridor to be paved, widened, and stripped of its soul to accommodate an endless flood of metal and smoke. The other vision recognizes that true development harmonizes human needs with ecological preservation. Ganderbal does not have a tree problem; it has a greed and management problem. Once those four Chinars are reduced to sawdust, they will never return in our lifetimes, nor in the lifetimes of our children. Yet, four years from now, the traffic jam on Duderhama Road will be back, worse than ever. Let us not sacrifice our living heritage on the altar of failed urban planning. True progress lies in fixing how we move, not destroying what keeps us alive. The writer is an educator from Ganderbal, Kashmir.

stories.headline: FPI buying hits 5-year high in November. What's driving the $7.5 billion inflow?
stories.title: FPI buying hits 5-year high in November. What's driving the $7.5 billion inflow?
stories.summary: Mumbai: In a sharp U-turn after months of sustained selling, foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) pumped $7.5 billion into Indian equities in the first 10 trading sessions of November - the highest monthly inflow in five years, according to Bloomberg data.This comes after FPIs withdrew $2.17 billion from Indian equities in October and $3.46 billion in September. The net investments in November so far are the highest since November 2021. The last time foreign investors pumped in more money in a single month was November 2020, when inflows stood at $9.56 billion, the data showed.135868866According to fund managers, FPIs have been aggressively investing amid a correction in AI-related stocks globally and a decline in crude oil prices. "The FPI flows are driven by multiple factors. profit booking on AI Investments, drop in oil prices, election results in Brazil, correction in Indian valuations over last two years, talks of exemptions on capital gains and reduction in rupee volatility," said Nilesh Shah, managing director of Kotak Mahindra AMC.All this came in quick succession and the combined effect is visible in FPI flows, he said.Read more: IPO calendar: Mahanadi Coalfields among 3 companies to raise over Rs 10,000 cr in busy week for primary marketBrent crude prices have fallen nearly 21% to $93.37 per barrel on November 13 from a peak of $118 on October 30. The Indian rupee has appreciated by ₹1.97, or about 2%, against the US dollar since the beginning of October, rising from ₹96.22 per dollar to ₹94.25 per dollar by mid-November.Domestic institutional investors, meanwhile, have turned net sellers, booking profits amid a sharp rally in the market, after providing a crucial backstop through much of the year. DIIs have sold equities worth over ₹49,000 crore in the first 10 trading sessions of November, according to NSE data. Since the beginning of November, the Sensex and Nifty have gained nearly 10% each, while the BSE MidCap 150 and BSE SmallCap 250 indices have advanced around 8% each.Read more: Will Sensex, Nifty continue their bull run or consolidate? 4 factors to watch out for this weekOverseas investors began 2026 with net outflows of $3.26 billion into Indian equities in January, before turning net buyers in February with investments of $1.69 billion. However, the respite was short-lived, as March saw a sharp reversal, with FPIs pulling out $13.23 billion - their biggest monthly sell-off.Their return to Indian equities reflects both global portfolio rotation away from AI-heavy markets and improving outlook for India, said Anurag Byas, director for global markets solutions at Rothschild & Co. "Lower crude prices, better earnings and now attractive valuations seem to have supported this sentiment change. This is a positive signal but may be early to be extrapolated; the fundamentals must improve and the oil and currency stability must hold for this to become a sustained trend," he said. Shah of Kotak Mahindra AMC expects FPI flows to move in line with how the above factors interplay with each other.
